items.body: Honoring its title, Justyna Jablonska‘s Unforeseen never heads exactly where expected; in fact, it’s not even close. The cellist’s debut solo album drips with the confidence of exploration, incorporating multiple genres while acting as a metaphor for the immigrant experience. Jablonska connects the migration of birds with the migration of people and the migration of oft-improvised notes, focusing on the lives of Ukrainian, Polish and Roma Gypsy migrants. While this seems like a lot to tackle, the artist does so with aplomb. The album begins as one might expect a cellist’s album to begin, with sedate phrasing, multitracked lines and a regal tone. The title track demonstrates Jablonska’s depth of emotion while establishing the baseline from which it will soon wander. Were the record to have continued in this vein, it would have remained exemplary; yet the artist strives for something greater, just as those dreaming for a better life might pack their belongings, imitating the flocks passing overhead in the spring and fall. As “If You Can Hear This” launches with a spoken word sample and jungle rhythms, all bets are off. The artist will not be confined by expectation. Is it safe? Not at all, and therein lies the appeal. The bird, the immigrant, the artist may each be called upon to adapt to new surroundings. “9 Daughers” is the first of three vocal pieces, beginning in birdsong and proceeding to a rendition of a traditional Lithuanian folk song A linden tree has nine branches, each one corresponding to a daughter, who each in turn are married, leaving the mother to “sweep the ashes.” The tone is one of mingled celebration and sadness: the empty nest, the broken tree. Can even the birds sing the sorrow away? The next piece starts with the sound of traffic, implying movement; then peaceful kalimba, cello and electronics, each in turn moving the music further away from its origins. The skies open in “Wayward,” and Jablonska seems forlorn, until a series of upbeat melodies are translated to percussion and string. These are the unforeseen joys of leaving the place where one has begun; by the end, the skies have cleared. But not all changes are easy; “Fabryka” introduces a brief note of dissonance, setting the listener up for Monika Niemczynowicz’s return on “The Pact,” an extremely dark cautionary tale from Roztocze, Poland. The presence of such songs underlines the connection between land, culture and memory ~ tales passed down generation to generation, even when the family has migrated to a new home. One hungers for the live show, incorporating film and copious amounts of spoken word, hinted at in the final minute of “Procession.” The album’s greatest surprise arrives toward the end with “Shchedryk (feat. Sofiia Fylypiv).” Most listeners will recognize “Carol of the Bells” in an instant, and many will recall its Ukrainian origins, but few will remember that the song predates Christianity and is about a swallow wishing a family “prosperity, good fortune and a fruitful year.” Jablonska reinstates the original title and meaning, reclaiming it from distortion. This too is a metaphor for the immigrant experience: the temptation to integrate to the extent that one’s history is sublimated. Jablonska, who lives in Glasgow, closes with her own take on “The Skye Boat Song,” which was itself adapted from a Gaelic tune. By the end, one is wondering about the the tug between one’s national origin and country of residence, and the very definition of home. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Simon Heath closes the release notes with “May you rest in peace.” There’s nothing to add to that. The Yasu Ether Project is an overall haunting and pleasant experience, a final document of an artist who understood that darkness and stillness aren’t opposites of beauty but conditions under which a particular kind of beauty becomes possible. César Alexandre knew that instinctively, and this album proves it one last time. A quiet closing chapter The Yasu Ether Project by Mount Shrine   Cryo Chamber has held the bar for exploratory dark ambient music with a cinematic edge since Simon Heath (the artist behind Atrium Carceri) founded the label with a collaborative focus that has become its defining characteristic. The catalog spans deep space drone, horror-influenced soundscapes, Lovecraftian collaborative projects, and the kind of patient, immersive dark ambient that rewards extended, solitary listening. Among its most beloved artists was Mount Shrine—the project of César Alexandre, a Brazilian producer from Rio de Janeiro who grew up absorbing Brian Eno, Burial, Aphex Twin, and Akira Yamaoka‘s score for Silent Hill 2 before finding his own voice in lo-fi field recordings, vinyl crackle, tape hiss, and long meditative drone structures. He debuted on Cryo Chamber with Winter Restlessness in 2018, followed by Ghosts on Broken Pavements in 2019. He also worked under Mount Hibiki and released vaporwave under the name Lindsheaven Virtual Plaza, an early and influential figure in that scene. César Alexandre passed away on April 15, 2021, from COVID-19. He was one of the first artists whose work made people fall in love with ambient music, and the void he left has been felt consistently in the years since. Cryo Chamber has honored his memory carefully—releasing All Roads Lead Home in 2022 and The Mount Hibiki Tapes in 2024, and The Yasu Ether Project arrives now as the final piece of audio he ever sent to Simon Heath. A version had previously appeared on his own Bandcamp before the page closed. Now preserved and released once more, it stands as a quiet closing chapter. There is a somber feeling that comes with reading about this release before you press play, and that feeling doesn’t leave once you do. Listening to this is the last remnant of his feelings and emotions, the final transmission from an artist whose music offered rest, solitude, and quiet escape to everyone who found it. Just like most Cryo Chamber releases you can expect a very dark and soft ride through the entirety of the album, but there is something that peaks through all the darkness, a simple peace that is haunting. You don’t know what it is that’s calming about it. Maybe it’s the field recordings of birds and daytime, the remembrance of what it feels like when you’ve just woken from a bad storm. Unsettling and peaceful at the same time. That’s how it feels listening to this. Unsettling and peaceful at the same time :: “Gaseous Peak” and “Polysunset” are the standouts on this release. The entirety of the album is wrapped in vinyl hiss, that persistent crackle that was always central to Mount Shrine‘s identity, the sound of something being played back from a medium that’s been worn down by time. It gives the record a physical texture, a sense that these recordings exist in a material world even as the music itself drifts away from one. The closing track is something different. The synths here aren’t just simple pads and atmospheric textures like the rest of the album. Little vocal touches, small nothings, barely registered, appear as the pads build. A small key arp plays in and out, and the visual being created in your head as you listen is genuinely peaceful in a way that feels earned after everything that preceded it. The contradiction at the heart of this closing track is what makes it so affecting, the familiar Mount Shrine darkness is still present, but something lighter has been let in, a crack of warmth that sits differently knowing what this release represents. Simon Heath closes the release notes with “May you rest in peace.” There’s nothing to add to that. The Yasu Ether Project is an overall haunting and pleasant experience, a final document of an artist who understood that darkness and stillness aren’t opposites of beauty but conditions under which a particular kind of beauty becomes possible. César Alexandre knew that instinctively, and this album proves it one last time. The Yasu Ether Project is available on Cryo Chamber. items.body: Six tracks, no wasted motion. ARKADA005 doesn’t revive electro; it plugs it back in, turns the voltage up, and lets the machine speak for itself. Drawing on the foundational grammar of electro Marking a welcome return to the furor of contemporary electronic music, London’s Arkada resurfaces with ARKADA005, a six-track workout from Brussels’ Arsonist Recorder and Sigma. This is electro with the futurist chrome stripped back enough to expose the working parts: rolling bass, snapping breaks, brutal low-end pressure and melodies that still know how to carry a tune. The record feels contemporary without straining to prove it, drawing on the foundational grammar of electro while treating that grammar as ​something alive, flexible and available for further damage. Arsonist Recorder takes the first three cuts straight to the machine soul. The rhythms are tight but never sterile, with heavyweight bass movement and synth lines that bring a real sense of propulsion. There is funk here, but it is not nostalgia-funk. It is the physical intelligence of the form: music built to make the body respond while the circuitry does something stranger underneath. Sigma answers with three tracks that feel like an autopsy performed at club volume. The components are stripped down, isolated and rebuilt into lean, muscular constructions where breaks, bass and synthetic detail lock together with increasingly brutal efficiency. What makes the record work is the tension between its opposing instincts—sweet melody and hard mechanics, precision and abrasion, body-popping unity and 4am chicanery. Six tracks, no wasted motion. ARKADA005 doesn’t revive electro; it plugs it back in, turns the voltage up, and lets the machine speak for itself. Arkada #005 is available on Arkada. items.body: Durable Oxide announces itself with DOX-001—the debut release from a new Portland, Oregon-based label intent on delivering decisive electronic atmospheres. It’s a strong opening statement for a label to make, and Radio Free Money earns it. Textured electronic music with an edge of menace Radio Free Money by Latest Fad   Durable Oxide announces itself with DOX-001—the debut release from a new Portland, Oregon-based label intent on delivering decisive electronic atmospheres. It’s a strong opening statement for a label to make, and Radio Free Money earns it. For a first release, the RIYL speaks volumes: Demdike Stare, Stars of the Lid, The Heartwood Institute, Castles In Space. That’s a specific compass pointing toward slow-burn, cinematic, deeply textured electronic music with an edge of menace, and Latest Fad delivers exactly that. Latest Fad is a duo—Paul Uusitalo and Dan Wilk, members based in Portland, OR and Seattle, WA, who have been collaborating on professional video software together for decades before turning their full attention to music in earnest in 2019. Their previous two albums came out on their own imprint Fading Systems. Radio Free Money is the​ir third full-length and their first on an outside label, employing banks of antiquated synthesizers, modern workstations, analog effects devices, and stringed instruments woven into an electroacoustic pastiche of submerged melodies, hidden rhythms, drops that never arrive, and hopeful/mournful atmospherics. The description “both claustrophobic and infinitely expansive” is apt—this is music that feels like it’s pressing in and opening outward at the same time. Simple ambience, but it works :: At first, Latest Fad is genuinely mysterious—you don’t know what to expect when you press play. This leans toward the ambient experimental side of things but has melodic aspects woven through. “Business Hugs II” arrives as the second track and introduces a static stutter effect that’s immediately intriguing, it opens a conversation the rest of the album keeps having with itself. This plays more as a collective than a conventional album, tracks functioning as interconnected environments rather than separate songs. “Overgrowth Mindset” is one of the most melodic pieces on the release—keys, off-rhythmic tones, and a bassline that brings some light into what is otherwise a consistently dark listening experience. Simple ambience, but it works as contrast against the heavier material surrounding it. “Aberrant Tool & Die” is another interesting piece—its only rhythm is a stable boom with a building single-note cymbal hit, that stale one-note repetition becoming hypnotic as other sounds and effects surface in the background before the track ends in a very dark place. Restraint is the operative word here. The track knows what not to do, and that’s half the work. “Live Laugh Loop” is the favorite of the release—a sad, dark melody with a flanged note sweeping in that makes the intro deliberately hard to parse. The distortion on the pads creates a density that almost obscures the other elements underneath, but those elements are there and they emerge gradually. Nothing here follows a conventional melodic pattern. The only thing obeying musical note rules is the distorted pads themselves—everything surrounding it is off-tone, and that off-tone quality is exactly what gives the track its dark, closing character. As a final statement it lands well. For a label’s debut release, Durable Oxide has set a clear and credible tone. Labels like Castles In Space and The Heartwood Institute built their identities one carefully chosen release at a time, letting the catalog define the aesthetic rather than announcing it upfront. DOX-001 suggests Durable Oxide understands that logic. Radio Free Money is a strong opening argument for what the label intends to be. Radio Free Money is available on Durable Oxide. items.body: From Helsinki’s Toinen kerros comes Isthmus Recordings, a new label and live archive capturing the restless, intimate sounds of Finland’s experimental music scene.   Bringing Helsinki’s Sounds Together Kesän korvalla by Koho / Koskenlahti Ballad Broadcast / Lineaments by Isthmus Recordings   Isthmus Recordings is a new record label based in Helsinki and Venice, also functioning as an archive for performances recorded in Toinen kerros, a new community-driven space for practicing and encountering sonic arts which which (in a few phases), has become a hub for the Finnish experimental music scene. The first two releases by Isthmus (directly funding the space with Bandcamp sales) include performances in genres such as electroacoustic improvisation, ambient, and minimalism. Recorded in May 2025 and fittingly titled Kesän korvalla—“on the verge of summer,” but also “with the ear of summer”—the first Isthmus release is a performance by the duo composed of sound artist J. Koho (whose brilliant designs grace the Isthmus cover arts so far) and percussionist Minna Koskenlahti. During the 35-minute piece, Koho / Koskenlahti improvise with amplified and processed concrète sounds, but also with sounds recalling more standard mallet percussion instruments and, later in the piece, wooden flutes and whistles. The improvised piece is organized in movements, with different moods and textures following one another: first frantic but gentle percussions set the atmosp​here, a drone-oriented phase follows and then vitalistic and almost free-jazz wind instruments loudly pierced the tapestry of drones. After this climax, the piece descends back into percussive territory, increasing in intensity and chaos and then falling back into order with long stretches of metallic sounds finally slowing down into ambiance. There is something meteorological about the piece, coming, growing and going like a weather event—a rush of wind moving natural and human objects before a summer shower, and then going and fading in the distance just as it came. Isthmus documents music in motion :: The second Isthmus release (Ballad Broadcast / Lineaments) so far includes two pieces, respectively a duo performance by Mark Reid Bulatović and Simone Spampinato, and a solo piece in two parts by Fredrik Rasten. The whole release focuses on guitars, and particularly acoustic guitars with uncommon tuning, interacting with ambience rather than effects or found sounds. At the beginning of Bulatović and Spampinato’s piece, “Ballad Broadcast,” the recording lets through room noise—a door opening, people moving, camera shutters—which, while most likely just accidental to the composition, add to the quiet and enigmatic guitar arpeggios. Over twenty minutes, the guitars form a very sparse call and response of sorts between a drier and more plucked sound and a strummed one with softer decay, but while they are in dialogue, they don’t offer an obvious interpretation, and the slice around them takes most of the sonic and semantic space. Fredrik Rasten’s piece, “Lineament” is a performance of the 2023 studio album of the same name. The pieces feature guitar arpeggios as the undisputed protagonists, but also held-note vocals and sine drones adding to the texture and interacting with the guitars’ own resonance and vibrations. While part I chooses simple arpeggios overlapping in their upward and downward trajectories as its main shape, in part two chords also enter the equation, giving a less regular effect and more space to the voice and drone. With forthcoming (and past) events at Toinen kerros including fantastic names both from the Finnish scene and internationally, one should really be looking forward to the live performance series growing—and hopefully more outside of the live archive too. (And if you’re in the Helsinki area, make sure to keep an eye on their programming!) Kesän korvalla and Ballad Broadcast / Lineaments are both available on Isthmus. items.body: Presumed finished after the death of founding member Richard H. Kirk, Cabaret Voltaire have instead returned to the stage with a vengeance, selling out shows, resurrecting old collaborations, and proving that their dark industrial pulse still hits hard in 2026. We caught up with Stephen Mallinder to talk about the reunion, the tour, Richard Kirk, and bringing the Cabs’ music back to life. Cabaret Voltaire rise from ashes But What Time Is It Really? by Cabaret Voltaire CODE (2026 Remastered Digital Deluxe Edition) by Cabaret Voltaire   For a group missing a founding member and presumed kaput for good after his death, Cabaret Voltaire have been busy. But 2026 has been a year of surprises and unexpected reunions. Among them, Cabaret Voltaire shines, with sold-out shows across Europe and the United States. Stephen Mallinder, one of the founding members, hit the stage with Chris Watson, who left the group in the 1980s, for an incredible tour of Europe. Now, Cabaret Voltaire returns to the States as they herald the re-release of CODE, their 1987 industrial dance masterpiece. “It’s been amazing to see the world again on tour,” said Mal as he prepared for their first show in the States on this last leg of their US tour. “The crowds ​are a great mix of people, with fans going way back as well as new fans. It’s been great to see younger folks at the shows really getting into it. Nice to see Cabaret Voltaire continues to bring people out.” Folks who want to hear how the band sounds after all this time can check out But What Time Is It Really?, a live recording from Cabaret Voltaire’s shows in the UK, including Sheffield, where it all began. Mal and company bring the classics to the stage with a new life and vitality. The songs sound very much like live versions fans will know, but with an updated edge that doesn’t rehash the material so much as enliven it, reminding us why their music became popular worldwide and remains so to this day. The themes and lyrics remain harshly relevant and resonant at a time when fascism isn’t being left behind closed doors anymore. “It was a concern when we were coming over to tour the West Coast,” said Mal when asked about visiting the States during a time of authoritarian crackdown. “We didn’t know what to expect. But it’s been okay and nothing out of sorts, really. No hassle playing—nothing like the old days when Mussolini Headkick came out and we had Nazi skinheads showing up to gigs! Those were rough, but we wanted to provoke people, to bring out a reaction, which we certainly did. But we’re not playing out-of-the-way places where people may not know our music. We’ve always played cities like New York, Chicago, or San Francisco, where we have a lot of longtime fans. But in San Francisco, for instance, there was a larger number of trans and gay kids at the show, which was great to see. People coming out to enjoy themselves and express themselves is always good for music and for us. Someone in Poland actually came to a gig dressed as the Microphonies cover, which was a first!”   Louder than ever :: On this leg of the tour, Mal is joined by Benge, a frequent collaborator with Mal among many others; longtime Cabs live member Eric Random; and Tara Busch, who takes over for Chris Watson, who will remain in the UK. “It’s been great playing with Chris again, as well as the rest of the band,” said Mal. “Chris and I are old friends, and we’ve played and toured together a lot. Nowadays it’s more or less the same, except his jokes are more shit than ever (laughs). But seriously, working with Chris and his massive collection of recordings has been incredible. It was interesting for him to learn songs that came after his time, not just ‘Landslide’ and ‘Nag Nag Nag.’ Since there were no stems to work from, Benge and I had to find all the samples with help from Chris.” “Since Chris is sitting out the US tour, Tara Busch has come onboard. Tara is a veteran, so having her come on was a no-brainer, as she’s toured with her band I Speak Machine and has worked with John Foxx and Benge as well,” said Mal. “She works the samples that Chris would, as well as handling other duties. I’ve played with Benge a lot, and Eric has been on The Crackdown and Microphonies as well as on tour with us. It’s a band of old friends.” With such longevity as the Cabs have had, it would be impossible to overlook the absence of Richard H. Kirk, who for several years after Mal’s departure kept use of the band name. As a founding member and one half of the band during their duo era, his absence from the tour is a sad one for fans and the band alike. “No, I don’t think so, sadly,” said Mal when asked if this tour would have been possible when Kirk was alive. “Richard wouldn’t have been interested in doing it with me. Though he did a few shows under the name, it was mostly his own work, from the later albums like Plasticity and International Language. He had an idea that Cabaret Voltaire could be an evolving, changing thing, but then he passed. And one of the things Chris and I wanted to do was not overlook him, but celebrate his part in the music of Cabaret Voltaire. It’s why we start the show with a dedication to him.” Cabaret Voltaire still make noise :: Having rehearsed and then toured the songs for almost a year, are there any plans to release material as the new Cabaret Voltaire? Mal isn’t circumspect. “It’s not like a novelty act or some rehashing of the old hits. In reworking the songs for the tour, we’ve made them so we can play them and have them recognizable, but they’re also new in a way, too. We’ve been recording the shows and lots of video from them as well. We will definitely be releasing some live stuff from it and other things.” The US dates coincide with Mute’s release of CODE, Cabaret Voltaire’s 1987 masterpiece and what some people consider the greatest work of their major-label dance days. “Mute did a fantastic job,” said Mal. “There’s so much material from then that we had to go through, with all the various mixes and remixes and demos from back then. CODE was probably our most overtly political record, which is interesting, touring and playing it in these very different but scary political times.”​ 2026 Final tour dates ::Sept 11 – Dallas, TX – Granada Theater^Sept 12 – Austin, TX – LevitationSept 15 – Chicago, IL –  Metro^Sept 16 – Chicago, IL –  Metro^Sept 18 – Toronto, ON –  Phoenix Concert Theatre^Sept 19 – Montreal, QC – Sat^Sept 21 – Boston, MA – The Wilbur^Sept 25 – New York, NY – Knockdown Center^Sept 26 – Philadelphia, PA –  Underground Arts^Oct 7 – Dublin, The AcademyOct 8 – Belfast, LimelightOct 10 – Birmingham, Town Hall*Oct 11 – Liverpool, Arts Club*Oct 13 – Nottingham, Rock City>Oct 14 – Cardiff, The Globe>Oct 15 – Bath, Forum*Oct 17 – Newcastle, Boiler Shop*Oct 18 – Glasgow, Barrowland*Oct 19 – Manchester, Albert Hall*Oct 21 – Bexhill, De La Warr Pavilion*Oct 22  – London, Roundhouse*Oct 25 – Sheffield, Octagon*^ w/ I Speak Machine*w/ Gazelle Twin> w/ Fader But What Time Is It Really? and CODE (2026 Remastered Digital Deluxe Edition) are both available on Mute. items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Embarking on an epic journey with a soundtrack playing in the background, that is the closest way to describe the experience of listening to Madness and Magic, the latest album by Arabs in Aspic. The opening track, "I Vow to Thee, My Screen," unfolds with an epic feel reminiscent of Rush, yet it also features symphonic touches and guitar-keyboard counterpoint characteristic of the most refined era of Genesis, featuring Steve Hackett and Tony Banks."Lullaby for Modern Kids, Part 1" creates a highly original acoustic atmosphere, aided by the percussion of the group's fifth member, Alessandro G. Elide. However, the organ and a choir lend an uncanny quality to the mood, as if stepping into a world imagined by Lewis Carroll, while a classical organ solo unfolds alongside a guitar part reminiscent of Pink Floyd. Masterfully employing psychedelic elements, the album addresses various types of addiction, to medication and new technologies, and how all of this distances us from reality; hence its detached, otherworldly quality, as if setting alienation itself to music. Perhaps we stop talking about it precisely when we are already deep within its grip."Lullaby for Modern Kids, Part 2" features delightful acoustic guitar work, and the echoes of early-era Gabriel return with striking force. The album offers a wealth of nuances and tonal colors, reflecting a range of modos, such as "High-Tech Parent," which evokes a Latin-tinged track by the Doobie Brothers. Fierce guitar work, accompanied by organ and percussion, creates moments of hypnotic rhythm, a soundscape the Norwegian quintet explores across both acoustic and electric dimensions.On "Madness and Magic," the interplay between Mellotron and synthesizers builds layers that pave the way for the album's centerpiece, "Heaven in Your Eye."Here, driven once again by synthesizers and Moog, the acoustic opening gives way to an ascent through inner and outer forests, a journey mirrored in the music and the highly expressive vocals. Dark, Black Sabbath-esque hard rock sections provide a stark contrast to Eastern-influenced melodies, where powerful riffs take command. The promise is ultimately fulfilled with sections of high dramatic tension, featuring distorted accelerations and organ followed by guitar, backed by Mellotron, like clouds accompanying lightning during a storm.

items.body: Few bands have achieved such a rapid development and enduring status in the Electronic music scene as Mesh. Founded in Bristol in 1991 by Mark Hockings and Richard Silverthorn, the British band evolved from a synth-driven group into an act with a highly distinctive blend of Electro-Pop, dark synth textures, subtle Rock influences, and deeply personal lyrics. From their earliest records, their music generated immense enthusiasm, which only continued to grow over the years. Their list of hits is almost too long to recount, and every new album generated a buzz. Following Neil Taylor’s departure in 2007, Mesh continued as the creative duo of Hockings and Silverthorn. Although a long period passed without a new studio album after the release of “Looking Skyward” (2016), Mesh never truly fell off the radar, largely because they continued to perform live. Eventually, the duo returned to the studio to begin writing new music. Their new album, “The Truth Doesn’t Matter (The Complete Truth)”, released on Dependent, marks Mesh’s ninth studio album. Despite the long hiatus, the band’s musical identity—or, indeed, its DNA—has remained completely intact. It is a strong record that stays true to the group’s distinctive sound and finest traditions. This interview took place during their current tour, which has also seen the band’s live lineup evolve. Mark and Richard are now joined on stage by drummer Sean Suleman and keyboardist Vaughn George. I reached out to Mark Hockings to look back briefly on 35 years of Mesh and, of course, to discuss the band’s current album and the road ahead. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Q: This year, you celebrate Mesh’s 35th anniversary, and your debut album “In This Place Forever” was released exactly 30 years ago. Which memories and absolute highlights immediately come to mind? Mark: It only seems like yesterday we started out, yet it really was a lifetime ago. I suppose our first album/EP “Fragile” getting made, our first shows in Bristol, our first shows in Sweden, our first shows in Germany, our first record signing to Memento Materia, our first big festivals, giving up work when we got signed to Orbit/Home Records, going on tour on a real tour bus, touring in the USA, every new album we ever released, every live show we ever played. As you can tell, we love it all. It’s been just one long adventure and we are still making memories. Q: Moving forward in time for a moment: it has been 10 years since you released a new studio album following “Looking Skyward”. That’s something we weren’t used to from you—how do you explain that gap, and when did you begin working on the new album? Mark: I think we just needed a bit of a break from writing and the whole album release cycle. It really is quite a commitment once you say ‘yes’ to a new album. It’s a lot of work and you have to be prepared to launch into it 100%. We did spend that time doing some writing, but we mostly played shows like the “Retrospective” tour and “The Point At Which It Falls Apart” re-release tour. We don’t consider any of this ‘lost’ time and was very valuable in further building up our following. We were able to come back to writing full of energy and fresh ideas. I think ultimately our releases this year will make up for the 10 years of waiting. Q: What formed the foundation of the ideas and influences behind “The Truth Doesn’t Matter – The Complete Truth”? Mark: It has not been difficult to find inspiration for this record. The rate of change of social and political norms has been unprecedented. We are in the middle of a huge technological shift that will forever change the way we work and communicate. The way that we all filter and process these changes will be key to how the World will look in the next few years. “The Truth Doesn’t Matter” is in parts a damning commentary on the World, but also offers hope for the future. If we can develop our skeptical skills and bring back some empathy then and we might just be OK. We are going through a huge learning period and I think we might just turn it all around. The mostly bland and disappointing use of all this new technology will hopefully give way to spectacular and life changing uses that will change all of our lives for the better. Q: With the album title, you seem to refer to so-called ‘post-truth’ realities. To what extent is this record an expression of criticism, or perhaps resignation—even acceptance—of that condition? And if truth no longer matters, what remains as a moral or emotional compass for humanity, and for artists who are, after all, only human? Mark: The title is more cynical than a statement of what I truly believe. It’s more of commentary on the ‘I believe this is true, and here are others that agree with me’ echo chamber type mentality that seems so have become gradually worse over time. The internet feeds such things of course. Ultimately the title suggests that you can actually spend your life mis-informed of basic truths and there is a high chance that your life will not be any worse for it because you will be in the company of the like-minded. On the face of it you could say that those people don’t matter and what is the harm in letting then be. But I’m not sure that these people are harmless. The danger comes when people try to re-write important social history or reverse the progress of technology, political leadership, social care, awareness and tolerance. So actually the truth does matter. It matters a lot. Q: Perhaps I’m misinterpreting certain titles, but songs like “I Lost A Friend Today” and “Trying To Save You” suggest more personal themes or experiences. What do these tracks convey exactly, and do they carry a deeper or more emotional significance for you? Mark: Yes, there are still personal songs on the album. “I Lost A Friend Today” is particularly personal. There needs to be room left for those intimate spaces on our albums I think. We rarely write an album completely based on a theme, but rather the theme exposes itself when the work is complete. We feel that the political, the emotional, the light and the dark can easily coexist on a single record and yet still present as a coherent piece. That coherence is as much to do with the construction of the music as the lyrics. Q: Despite the melodic and danceable nature of your music, there has always been a darker, melancholic undercurrent. I find it fascinating how these elements coexist—people dancing intensely to songs that deal with serious themes. How do you view that contrast? Mark: I think we’ve always tried focus on the emotional side of all of our tracks. Yet is important to us to create energy if it helps to push that emotion to the fore. It can seem like a dichotomy when analysed in this way, but to us it has always made perfect sense to us. There are quiet emotions and there are loud emotions. There are sad emotions and there are angry emotions. It’s a spectrum that requires a different musical backdrop every time. Q: In a world that often seems to be deteriorating, Art—including music—serves as an outlet and a source of hope. At the same time, we see increasingly conservative governments and world leaders cutting funding for the Arts. How do you interpret this contradiction, and how do you see the role of Art and music evolving? Mark: It may be true that the funding of publicly funded art is generally being cut all over the World, however it feels like there is more creativity out there than there has ever been. People are able to make great music, film and art with the cheapest of tools. They have free platforms that give them an outlet for that art. I think you just have to go and find it. Gone are the days when a small number of intellectuals influence the way our culture moves. There are very few blockers in your way if you want to make art in some form. Most people are not out to make money, or become famous doing this. It just makes them happy. I think this is a really great thing. We just have to re-adjust the way we discover art and music. It just requires a little more effort possibly. But isn’t that part of the fun? Q: At a time when everything is accelerating and constantly evolving, I sometimes wonder what purpose an album still serves. With streaming platforms and algorithm-driven playlists and social media dominating how people listen to music, does releasing an album become a form of resistance—a deliberate ‘no’ to that evolution? Mark: We still think it’s important to give people a coherent piece of work. To take an idea and run with it. We still like the format of the physical album, the journey, the depth, the story, the artwork. The album set a theme like a film or a book. The songs are the scenes or the chapters. Hopefully the album tells a story and the listener is left with an experience or a memory when they listen to it a whole. We understand that things are moving possibly in a different direction, but I don’t think this a denial thing, like being resistant to new technology or delivery platforms. I believe that people are genuinely missing out on the album format as a way of consuming music, and I think that streaming services could do more to make music more of an experience. Q: As mentioned earlier, it has been 10 years since your previous studio album. Has your way of collaborating changed during that time? And how have studio practices or production tools evolved for you—especially with the rise of technologies like AI? Mark: Collaboration tools have improved certainly. Our main program Cubase has a remote client that we use when working with our mix engineer Olaf in Germany. This is partially made possible due to faster network connections available now. A lot of retro gear is cheaper and more available due to companies like Behringer. Controversial possibly, but they have made expensive classic synths affordable to a lot of people. A.I has certainly made mastering tools a lot easier to use for final productions, but we tend to still rely on the skills of people like Olaf to deal with that still. Tools like Suno AI, particularly Suno studio might have their place in bringing ideas to the table, but those platforms are still a little predicable in their results. Ultimately I suspect we will use such things to generate sounds and loops not unlike using sample packs or services like splice. I don’t see anything wrong with any of this stuff really. Ultimately the artist is the filter for ideas and where those ideas come from is largely irrelevant. Exciting times though. Q: The album features several short interludes. What role do they play within the broader context of the record? And could you also tell us more about the album’s Deluxe Edition? Mark: The interludes we call “Particles” and are used to add a bit of colour to the record or to change moods in the flow. When you take the confines of the lyrics out of the equation then you can be a little more free in the way you manage the structure of those pieces. We are able to try a few sound design experiments that would be difficult if words were involved. So they are just little mood changing experiments that are fun to write. The deluxe edition contains a few tracks that we either couldn’t fit on the physical CD/vinyl or we didn’t think necessarily fitted on the album quite as well as the final track list. That is subjective obviously, but we spend a long time considering such things. That said, I love the additional tracks on the extended version. Q: Is there a particular stereotypical modus operandi when it comes to creating a song or an album, or how does that process actually work—more specifically for the new album? Mark: Not really. We just swap ideas and see what happens. The difficult part is just getting started. We need a couple of good songs finished before the ball really starts to roll. Generally Rich will give me some music and I’ll write a song around that, or I’ll make a demo and Rich will work on it. But the process varies. We get together to work on final vocals, final mixes, final arrangements etc. It’s much more collaborative towards the end of the process than at the start. We tend to need to get together a nucleus of tracks and then step back and see a) where is this going? And b) what are we missing? But tracks sometimes just appear out of nowhere – like “Exile” for example. This was written after we’d mixed the final album and was added at the very last minute. Happy accidents or hard work? Difficult to be sure. Q: At the time of this interview, you’ve already played a lot of live shows, and the tour is still ongoing. What have been the highlights so far? What do you enjoy most about touring and performing in different countries, at different festivals, and in a variety of venues? Mark: The highlights have been the people and the enthusiasm and love they have shown us. It’s been quite humbling. Can never get used to it. We pushed ourselves to make this tour a really special production and I think we surpassed our expectations on how the show looked and sounded. Touring is just fun. We love the whole process to be honest. The shows, the fans, the travelling in the tour bus, the friendship and the shared experience. Every venue is different, every crowd is different. Festivals can be fun, but a very different thing as the audience is not necessarily there to see you. Its a different challenge, but just as rewarding off you get it right. Q: I’ve always wondered how a band prepares for a tour like this. What’s involved in getting everything ready? Could you also tell us a bit about the crew that travels with you? And when you’re not on stage, how do you spend your time on the road, and what do you do to stay in good shape throughout the tour? Mark: There are months of preparation involved in a tour like this. The music has to be completely reprogrammed for live, hardware and software has to be prepared/written especially for the tour. Video plays a big role in our stage show and this also takes months to author and sync to the live sequencing. So essentially we are straight out of the studio from the album, then straight back into it again. There are a huge amount of logistics involved around video, lighting, merch, crew, travel, support bands etc. it’s a huge undertaking. We have the best crew and many of them we have worked with for many, many years. I think there were 14 of us on the bus for this tour. Touring seems to be a lot of hanging about interspersed with intense periods of activity. But the time passes too fast. It’s a lot of fun. We all keep reasonably fit. Myself and Rich do a lot of cycling. Sean does a lot of gym work. You can’t do. Much once you are actually on tour, so the prep is important.

items.body: The Cure released their sixth studio album, “The Head on the Door,” on 30 August 1985 through Fiction Records. The album turns 41 this year. It followed 1984’s “The Top” and arrived with a lineup that added drummer Boris Williams and brought back bassist Simon Gallup and guitarist Porl Thompson. The band recorded “The Head on the Door” in 1985 at Angel Recording Studios in London. Robert Smith and David M. Allen produced the album, with Howard Gray producing “Kyoto Song,” “Push” and “A Night Like This,” and Frank Barretta engineering. The ten-track record runs “In Between Days,” “Kyoto Song,” “The Blood,” “Six Different Ways,” “Push,” “The Baby Screams,” “Close to Me,” “A Night Like This,” “Screw” and “Sinking.” It was issued on vinyl LP and CD, led by the single “In Between Days,” which reached number 15 on the UK Singles Chart, and followed by second single “Close to Me.” “The Head on the Door” reached number seven on the UK Albums Chart and number 59 in the US, and is certified gold in the US, UK and France. It streams on Spotify. About The Cure The Cure formed in Crawley, England, in 1976, when school friends Robert Smith and Lol Tolhurst played together in a band that became Malice, then Easy Cure. Easy Cure signed briefly to the German label Ariola-Hansa in 1977, but the deal collapsed in 1978 after the label rejected the song “Killing an Arab” and pushed for cover versions instead. Guitarist Porl Thompson was dropped from the lineup in April 1978, and Smith renamed the remaining trio the Cure. Later that year, Polydor scout Chris Parry signed the band to his newly formed Fiction label. The Cure released the single “Killing an Arab” in December 1978 and its debut album, “Three Imaginary Boys,” in May 1979. Bassist Simon Gallup joined for “Seventeen Seconds” (1980), an album that helped shape the emerging gothic rock sound, followed by “Faith” (1981) and “Pornography” (1982). Gallup left after the “Pornography” tour, and Smith put the Cure on hold to join Siouxsie and the Banshees as guitarist. Tolhurst switched from drums to keyboards, and the pair released the singles “Let’s Go to Bed” (1982), “The Walk” and “The Love Cats” (1983), later compiled on “Japanese Whispers.” For 1984’s “The Top,” Smith played most of the instruments himself, drummer Andy Anderson and early Malice member Porl Thompson filled out the sessions, and Thompson officially rejoined the band. During the following tour, Boris Williams, previously the touring drummer for Thompson Twins, became the Cure’s official drummer, and Gallup rejoined after reconciling with Smith. This lineup of Smith, Tolhurst, Gallup, Williams and Thompson recorded “The Head on the Door” in 1985, and the album’s success carried into the “Standing on a Beach” singles compilation the following year. The Cure went on to release “Kiss Me, Kiss Me, Kiss Me” (1987), “Disintegration” (1989) and “Wish” (1992), and were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2019. The band’s most recent studio album, “Songs of a Lost World,” arrived in November 2024 after a 16-year gap, followed by the remix collection “Mixes of a Lost World” in June 2025. The Cure returned to Rockfield Studios in March 2025 to record 13 songs for a follow-up album, placing “The Head on the Door” anniversary within an active chapter of the band’s ongoing work.

items.body: Nine Inch Nails released “Hesitation Marks” on 30 August 2013 through The Null Corporation, distributed by Columbia Records in the United States and Polydor Records elsewhere. The eighth studio album by Trent Reznor‘s industrial rock project turns 13 this year. It was the band’s first full-length release in five years, following 2008’s “The Slip,” and its only album distributed through Columbia. “Hesitation Marks” was produced by Reznor alongside Atticus Ross and Alan Moulder, Reznor’s longtime studio collaborators; it remains the most recent Nine Inch Nails album to be co-produced by Moulder. The standard edition runs 14 tracks: “The Eater of Dreams,” “Copy of a,” “Came Back Haunted,” “Find My Way,” “All Time Low,” “Disappointed,” “Everything,” “Satellite,” “Various Methods of Escape,” “Running,” “I Would for You,” “In Two,” “While I’m Still Here” and “Black Noise.” Guest musicians on the record include Lindsey Buckingham, Adrian Belew, Pino Palladino and Ilan Rubin. Tom Baker handled mastering. Cover art across the album’s several editions was created by Russell Mills, the artist behind the visuals for “The Downward Spiral” nineteen years earlier. Three singles preceded the album: “Came Back Haunted” (June 6, 2013), “Copy of a” (August 13, 2013) and “Everything” (August 20, 2013). “Hesitation Marks” debuted at number three on the Billboard 200 and topped the Canadian Albums Chart, and was nominated for the Grammy Award for Best Alternative Music Album at the 56th Annual Grammy Awards. About Nine Inch Nails Nine Inch Nails was formed by Trent Reznor in 1988 in Cleveland, Ohio. Reznor wrote, arranged and performed nearly all instrumentation on the band’s debut album, “Pretty Hate Machine,” released via TVT Records in 1989. After a dispute with TVT over promotion, Reznor signed with Interscope Records and released the EP “Broken” in 1992, followed by “The Downward Spiral” (1994) and “The Fragile” (1999). Nine Inch Nails returned from a hiatus with “With Teeth” (2005) and “Year Zero” (2007), then left Interscope and independently released the instrumental double album “Ghosts I-IV” and “The Slip,” both in 2008, before entering a second hiatus. Reznor announced the return of Nine Inch Nails in February 2013 and confirmed on May 28, 2013 that a new album, recorded in secret with Atticus Ross and Alan Moulder, was finished. That record, “Hesitation Marks,” followed on August 30, 2013, backed by the Twenty Thirteen Tour featuring Reznor, Ross, Robin Finck, Alessandro Cortini, Josh Eustis and Ilan Rubin. Ross, previously a production collaborator, became an official member of Nine Inch Nails in 2016. Subsequent releases include the EPs “Not the Actual Events” (2016) and “Add Violence” (2017), the album “Bad Witch” (2018), and “Ghosts V: Together” and “Ghosts VI: Locusts,” both released in 2020. Nine Inch Nails was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2020. “Hesitation Marks”, the album that ended the band’s second hiatus, turns 13 this year.

items.body: The German duo Arnte and Schmoun—formerly active together as Nordschlacht and Ugh, but having operated as Pyrroline for years—are releasing their fifth album, “Ambiguity”. The work appears inspired by the world we live in and, above all, by the impact of various events on the human psyche. Musically, this translates into 12 tracks that immediately reveal the signature Pyrroline sound. The group remains closely linked to the musical legacy of early Skinny Puppy. Hovering somewhere between sophisticated EBM and atmospheric Dark-Electro, this new opus once again succeeds in captivating the listener. A dark, frenzied atmosphere is established, underpinned by complex percussion. At times, the mood is somewhat tormented, yet that is precisely the strength of certain tracks. The polished production features a wealth of sounds and subtle effects, layered with ghostly vocals. Here and there, female vocals appear, adding a touch of cold sensuality. One of the tracks also features a collaboration with TC75. “Ambiguity” may not be the band’s strongest album—their previous release, “Struggling”, was a masterpiece, after all—but it remains a powerful record from a group that, in my opinion, continues to be somewhat underrated. (Rating:8). Listen to “Eventually”: https://electroaggressionrecords.bandcamp.com/track/eventually

items.body: Toronto-based duo Kazdoura debuted their single “Taa” on COLORS, taking their Levantine psych-rock to the platform’s bare monochrome stage. for a stripped set putting the song’s guitar and voice fully in view. The track opens on intricate guitar motifs over an ominous chord progression, before a steady drum groove settles underneath. Leen Hamo‘s vocal carries the phrasing of vintage Arabic pop, floating over the arrangement as it tightens through the verses and opens into a chorus built on a hypnotic, ride-cymbal-led rhythm. Hamo, who is Syrian, and Lebanese multi-instrumentalist John Abou Chacra formed Kazdoura in Toronto. The name means “to stroll” in Levantine Arabic, and the JUNO Award-winning duo draw on Arabic maqam melodies while layering in psychedelic soul, jazz and funk. The lyrics deal with memory and the difficulty of letting go. The COLORS premiere opens a European run that starts at Spillestedet Stengade in Copenhagen on August 28 and the Habibi Funk Festival in London on August 29 and 30. From there the duo plays the Jam Jar in Bristol on September 3, Norwich Arts Centre on September 4, Peggy’s Skylight in Nottingham on September 6, and a show in Istanbul on September 11, before Paradiso in Amsterdam on September 15 and the Reeperbahn Festival in Hamburg on September 17 and 18. items.body: Summer is ending. We must not say this out loud; it is a hard pill to swallow. For many people, summer has already ended; vacations are over, classes have begun, the water has cooled. zakè‘s Tide Requiem for the Low Sea is a long, slow, poignant goodbye, holding on until the very last moment, like the last bit of a small island before it is submerged. The physical representation is gorgeous: a double-sided picture disc, suitable for framing, showcasing photography by Tom Meluch (Benoît Pioulard). The images inspired both the music and their titles. One can imagine clinging to one of these peaks, like Blake Lively in “The Shallows,” albeit with more sadness than drama. Each side contains a single track, logging in at 22:46. The title track occupies Side A, ebbing in and out like the tide. Precious piano notes float atop the layered, undulating drones. Time seems be in suspension, although this is an illusion; it is simply passing slowly and inexorably from summer to autumn. Larger chords pass like behemoths in the sea, never quite surfacing, as much a feeling as they are a presence. How long can one hold on before succumbing to the sea? The answer should be six hours, the distance between high and low tides, and while we are not requesting a six-hour recording, it would be interesting to experience. A quarter-day at the beach allows for nuance, for incremental change that eventually grows extreme. “Tide Requiem for the Low Sea” seems to reflect the ocean at its lowest, before the rising tide, when one is aware that time is limited. The complementary “Crimson Covenant” is like a different viewpoint of a similar scene or like two persons comparing notes. Is the tide advancing or receding, and is the glass half full or half empty? If there is value to be found in each, might it also be applied to the changing seasons? The chords are darker, as one might expect from the title, which (likely coincidentally) is shared with an RPG. They advance and recede more swiftly, like the reduced interval between waves. The organ-like tones contribute elegance and gravity. Funeral offers music as a bridge between worlds; this piece suggests a similar metaphor. One of the unique curiosities of the record (as opposed to the download) is that the needle grows ever closer to an island peak, beginning at the outskirts as it alternately treads water and rests on land. The implication is that even the needle is seeking safety from the tide, and eventually finds it. The same may be true for the listener, leaving the seas of summer and landing safely on the shores of fall. (Richard Allen)

A cinematic ascent that feels simultaneously weightless Cicada Burnt by leo   Leo‘s latest six-track EP, Cicada Burnt, is a stunningly crafted collection of teknoid soundscapes where cutting-edge pulses scatter love bullets of intent with serious depth, weight and imagination. If electronic music came as cakes, this would be a deeply delicious one: richly layered, beautifully balanced and full of rewarding detail with every return. Expansive atmospheres form the broad canvas upon which pole and wood basslines stutter in and out of half-time, dub-inflected drops, while slack hi-hats and clipped synth motifs generate an insistent sixteenth-note tension that constantly nudges the music forwards without ever overcrowding it. Opener “Qwershapes” immediately establishes the EP’s language, balancing precision with abandon in a thrilling display of rhythmic confidence and sonic restraint. “Jetti” follows by treating emptiness, timing and negative space as instruments in themselves, exemplifying the post-genre spirit increasingly defining contemporary elec​tronics. Rather than merely hopping between stylistic traditions from one track to the next, Leo folds those traditions into individual compositions, dissolving tribal boundaries with the confidence of an artist more interested in expression than categorization. The title track is a genuine low-end masterwork. Wah-soaked synths, sculpted percussion, clipped rhythmic fragments and heavyweight bass converge into something simultaneously playful and profound, expressing the paradox that the deepest seriousness often reveals itself through the joy of creative play. It is music that feels instinctive rather than calculated, communicating an artistic presence that cannot simply be learned. “Descant” reinforces that philosophy through muscular bass pressure and hypnotic propulsion before the closing two-part “Spirit Level” reaches the record’s emotional summit. “Prescript” inhabits an elusive territory between ambience, dub, found sound and bass music without settling into any recognizable form, its immense scale matched by genuine warmth. The concluding piece channels skyscraper tension, unstable bass movements, dub-wise pyrotechnics and voice-like pads into a cinematic ascent that feels simultaneously weightless and earthbound. Superb work, and comfortably one of the finest releases in Leo‘s growing catalog. Cicada Burnt is available on Peak Oil. items.body: Northern Earth is a fully instrumental, sprawling and contemplative sound journey of minimalist, solitary-mood pieces which deserve patience and spiritual disposition. Mystical devotion and cinematic splendor Northern Earth by Dean McPhee   Dean McPhee is a sound artist and a guitarist apart from restricted stylistic categories. His musical production spans more than a decade with steady releases on some obscure indie labels. His last efforts have been released under his own publishing structure: Bass Ritual. Released in 2011, his album for Blast First Petite (owned by Paul Smith of Mute) is unfortunately the only one I got familiar with, but I will definitely try to correct this lack of knowledge. Comparing this older work with the new offer, we might say that McPhee rapidly found his musical path back then, mixing with skills, spirit and evocativeness a chilling emotional psychedelic folk mantra with hypnotic looped effects obtained with guitars. Northern Earth follows a relatively similar path, with an emphasis on repetitive and ritualized guitar-centered soundscapes of heavenly and spiritual beauty behind more raw textured motifs. In a way, it reminds me of lonesome krautrockin’ excursions from the 70s with Popol Vuh, Ash Ra Tempel, or even Fripp/Eno lyergic grooves (in the self-titled track), but here the whole thing embraces a sense of existential wandering, natural vastness, mystical devotion and cinematic splendor. Rolling percussive pulses and nuanced effects :: The guitar is generally soaked in a heavy pack of reverbs, also turning on slightly relaxing slide style, alternating sinuous textures with moody-esque repetitive melodies that will lead you in a beatific state. Rare sound objects, rolling percussive pulses and nuanced effects punctuate the body of tracks. I must say it is a welcoming surprise and a break from the too ambient-ish electronic efforts I reviewed recently. Absolutely recommended for fans of Cosmic Americana (as a musical subgenre), Pan•American, Stars of the Lid, Labradford, Saadé. It would have made a nice soundtrack for some road movies and slow-moving western-themed films by Jim Jarmusch or Kelly Reichardt in Meek’s Cutoff’ Northern Earth is a fully instrumental, sprawling and contemplative sound journey of minimalist, solitary-mood pieces which deserve patience and spiritual disposition. items.body: Across eight tracks, Germano channels a stunning miasma of electronic and acoustic instrumentation, art-house aesthetics, and installation-worthy musical spaces. Balancing precision with emotional ambiguity opera23 is Vincenzo Germano who, after an apparent three-year hiatus, returns to Wic Recordings with Teatro Armónico—a valiant, mature statement of adult aural dynamics. Across eight tracks, Germano channels a stunning miasma of electronic and acoustic instrumentation, art-house aesthetics, and installation-worthy musical spaces. Grand piano discordance sits alongside elevated musicianship, while glitch techniques fracture and elevate the compositions rather than simply decorate them. Every movement feels carefully considered, balancing precision with emotional ambiguity. Rather than chasing convention, Teatro Armónico unfolds as a sequence of immersive environments where composition, texture, and silence carry equal weight. Organic performances dissolve into digital erosion before reforming in unexpected ways, creating a dialogue between the human hand and machine inter​vention. The result is music that rewards patient listening, revealing new details with every return. This is neither academic abstraction nor easy ambience. Germano occupies the fertile ground between contemporary classical composition, electroacoustic experimentation, and sound art, producing an album that is intellectually engaging without sacrificing feeling. Teatro Armónico is a quietly commanding return—one that confirms opera23 as an artist more interested in lasting resonance than fleeting impact. TEATRO ARMÓNICO is available on Wic. items.body: Review by tszirmay — Nine years after their underwhelming 2025 'Beast, Machine & Man', this Finnish combo returns with 'Monologue of Chronos' with the home of reigniting the rave reviews for their 2006 debut 'Armed Forces of Simantipak' as well as the follow-up 'Disconcerto Grosso' , both most enjoyable recordings . Essentially now a trio of Atte Kurri, Ilkka Piispala and Ilkka Saarikivi, all pretty much multi-instrumentalists, as well as participating in the vocal department, this is quite the tight package containing seven mid-sized tracks. A wide variety of keyboards usurp the stage, the main motor in composing and creating the appropriate sonic groundwork, while the rhythm section remains lively within the process. The end result is perhaps closer to more progressive versions of 10cc or even Supertramp, pretty overt in the vocal harmonies that made the two bands in questions such powerhouses. Thrown in burly bass guitar settings, and pumping piano, organ and synthesizer motifs with impunity and you get the picture. One immediate observation is that the harmonies clearly outshine the lead vocals, which can be a tad reedy and thin at times, it's an oddity that does not condemn the arrangements in any manner. As befits a monologue I guess, there are no uneven tracks here, as all seven form a setlist with enough diversity and instrumental technique that have both Neo and Symphonic characteristics. On occasion, the screeching guitar leaps out and bites, on others it's the obdurate bass lines that provide the thrills, a modern approach that eschews any need for senselessly flashing solos, preferring amore cohesive overall experience. After the first two tracks set the standard and the pace, the album really starts hitting its groove on the relentless 'The Dystopian Spirit of Club Energy', the instrumental core attracting quite a few raised contented eyebrows. This impression blooms even further on the impressive 'Song of Days', a pummelling onslaught that delivers the goods, a poignant drum beat in particular doing a fair amount of damage, as if urging the symphonics to take over, while shifting the urgency at will, keeping the drama intense. The cute Yes-isms are both adorable and reverential, the slippery axe solo a total blast and the percussion throughout subtle and a propos. These two tracks easily outduel the aging affirmative crew as well as those Asia guys. Me like this. 'DID Memoir' introduces a gorgeous piano within a melody to die for, bold and adventurous, as the development takes the tempo into a comfort zone, a prog power ballad! The keyboards have an echoing tone that is most modern and utterly appealing. On a dime, the switch is momentarily flipped and a jazzier mood hits one right between the ears! Another button is pressed and the rush returns like a long-withheld memory. A semi-rap section had me fall off my chair, a clever little insert that clicked on all cylinders. The intertwined vocal harmonics come back for an encore on 'The Keepers of Philosopher's Stone', the piano and bass playing together, as if building sandcastles on the beach, the assorted keyboardists doing a few Gentle Giant stylistics to confuse the audience. There is an ongoing battle between complex arrangements, loaded with experimentation, such as the harpsichord patch, veering into an organ splurge that would make Kerry Minnear smile and a sense of accessibility that dares not to give way to familiarity.Well appointed theatrics appear on the finale 'Mundus Meus (This World of Mine)', so as it leave a positive last impression. It's also the longest track by a few seconds, with a stunning chorus and a series of wicked guitar abrades, a fitting example of nailing the deal. The neo-Gregorian choir bit really hit the spot. An entertaining modern prog album that deserves a commitment to listen with an open mind, and enjoy all of its constructive attributes. A few spins will get it done. 4 Armenian speeches

items.body: Review by HogweedOfTuscany — aka "the most irresistible album I've ever hated."The story of Marillion and their transformation is something that doesn't need any further explanations or elaborations ... not in 2026, at least. It took me a long, very long time to fall in love in their "latter" era (which easily dwarfs their early era by now, whether in years or in albums, and can be therefore quite safely considered their "main" or "primary" era by even the most rabid Fish aficionados) and to be perfectly honest, Brave can be at least partially blamed for that.As a friend of mine had put it once, "Brave is what Marillion sounds like to people who hate Marillion" and I can't stop thinking about that. Brave has the iconic album cover, the iconic concept, the reputation of being one of the Hogarth-era Marillion's undisputable highlights - it could be arguably considered the most famous oeuvre of the Fishless band. And it is also a dour, brooding, static, soft and quiet, melodyless dirge that would put a chainsaw to sleep. And no, although I love the album now, after years of being obsessed with it despite hating it, I won't mince my words. Brave may be - for all its unassuming qualities and the almost mainstream sound - one of the most unwelcoming albums I have ever heard, comparable to Trout Mask Replica, even. At first, it's just a drone - so post-rockish that it becomes almost half-ambient, slow, quiet and absolutely unmemorable. There are songs that completely lack discernible structure (and opening the album with one of them - Living with the Big Lie - is certainly an artistic choice) and even those that are lively and could be almost considered catchy (Lap of Luxury, Paper Lies and Hard as Love, which all sounds like the band has been provided a rejuvenated bolt of cocaine as if Fish wandered back into the studio to greet old friends and forget some powder behind) are mercilessly sabotaged by the production, which is so tinny and weak that the songs just do not work that way. I won't lie to you, after three listens, pretty much all I could remember from this 70+ minute album was: A. hogarth's histrionics as he shouts the title very near the end of Living with the Big Lie, B. that Rothery's wistful, almost pastoral guitar part on Runaway, C. Lap of Luxury chorus, D. "Baby, nothing else has ever been as hard as love", E. the bagpipes on the title track. The rest was all a mush and a definite proof that Marillion have finally metamorphosed into a fully post-rock ensemble, deciding that everything should be subjugated to the amoebous, indifferent cruel mistress called "atmosphere". I hated the album.And yet, I came back. Not that I would necessarily remember that much more with repeated listens and not that I would particularly enjoy the bleak mood of the album (I like me some melancholy, sure, but it has to be meaningful melancholy), but somehow I couldn't stay away. Brave became the dragon I had to slay, in order to appreciate Harillion and understand why the fans are so obsessed they travel half the globe to watch them perform this in full on a Marillion weekend, or why their fanclub releases are so bizarrely numerous. Every few months or so, I'd put this weird album with the weird blurred bird on the cover and the indecipherable themes - starting with the album title - and I was obsessed with how I didn't get it. I don't know when it clicked for me. In fact, I'm not even sure IF it clicked for me, or if I've just somehow abused my mind so as to embrace the album like a true contrarian. The album is like the river Severn, really. You see a tiny single wave that you like, but you can't really identify it, you can't keep watching it; it will disappear out of sight. It's a mass, a flow, a churning, but really unchanging, unthinking volume of water. You can call the river stupid, but it will be there once you've been gone. The only thing that remains is the option to consider drowning yourself in it, as so many have before. And be called Brave by Hogarth for that consideration. I don't know what to say about this album, my musical words fail me. I think I love it, but I don't know why. However, don't give up, when all is said and done, it's pretty cool. Hypnotic, even. If you wish to get into hogarth-era Marillion, though, maybe go for a different album first, like Marbles.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — Milanese quintet releases their third album, following their 2017 debut "Alight" and "Nautilus" which came two years later, both well received. The band continues to feature vocalist Francesco Lovari (whose English is as great as his lung capacity) , Alessandro Palmisano handling all matters guitar, Niccol� Gallani shuffling his keyboard arsenal while the family tandem of Loris Bersan on bass duties and Eric Bersan doing the drums and percussion chores. Nine years and no line-up changes, lovely move! "Wasted Potential" is a clever opening title that has zero bearing on the music proposed here, introducing the blustering keys, the thrilling voice, the rhythmic duo in full force and a shrugging guitar shroud, with less than 5 minutes, preciously condensed and intense. This is moder RPI, firmly ensconced in the schizoid 21st century, freshly brash and slash. A tremendous sizzler. Following that slap in the face with a sense of humour-laden "Please Be Gentle" is a proof positive that no one does drama better than our Italian Fratelli! Once again, the savvy interplay shows a team spirit that can only be admired (since the 'squadra' sucks lately, this is all one can have!), Gallani's moaning mellotron forging massive choral swoops, the bass and guitar smashing harshly and the percussive thuds very remote from tender facility. 2 shots, 2 goals, time for an epic! The 11 and a half minute long "The Case of the Silent Queen" evokes pastoral emanations of acoustic splendour (early Genesis and Anthony Phillips), the delicate arrangement increasing in intensity at a 'gentle' pace, the exuberant piano and drum cooperation making this a most flavoursome affair, the symphonics kicking in with romantic glee, as the mellotron keeps on glowing. The transitional variations are subtle, keeping the emotional impact well entrenched between the ears, dabbling bits of choir and thrashing cymbals awakening the soul. Suddenly, the not-too silent explosion arrives, led by an obsessive synthesizer loop, hushed vocal effects, and occasional axe-driven slashes that thunder without remorse. With all cylinders revving mightily, the lister's pulse cannot help racing forward into another realm of consciousness, no hint of filler or dross, just straight on musical theater for the demanding prog fan. Absolute master class demonstration. A little well-deserved respite is called for, after such a harrowing experience. "We Need to Talk" is exactly that, an effortless human grievance, we all have endured too many times. Heartbreak, heartache, loss, separation, distance, fate, called it what you will. The lyrics take their warranted place , upfront and center, as if "it was meant to be". A stunning vocal chorale, Palmisano shining on acoustic, Gallani burning on his keys, the Bersans keeping it all tightly wrapped in bliss. "Caged" is the other longer track, and as the title suggests , it's a heavily claustrophobic musical enclosure, the hyper piano possessed throughout, Lovari singing like an incarcerated victim of circumstance, no access to a phone or a ticket to freedom. We are stuck in limbo, and all alone. The screeching guitar solo secretes the angst for the longing of escape, the bass desperately searching for a way to open the locks, leading to the outside. When those damned mellotrons blow the roof off the penitentiary , the raging guitars in full collusion, the deed is done. Free at last. Maintaining the focus on the human condition, "The Day We Never Met" offers a jazzier vibe, weighed down by brooding e-piano and synth evolutions, a lovely contrast between melody and dissonance, but within a completely different style compared to the rest of the album. You may have guessed by now, and yes, the sturdy mellotron once again blows into the midst with thunderous resilience. Extraordinarily seductive. The title track puts this exceptional album to rest, a well-deserved siesta after a completely entertaining performance. As a fitting finale, the piece sort of encompasses the underlying thrill of the entire album, strengthening the beliefs in the talent presented here. Its everything one may want from modern day progressive rock. Please continue, and never get out of you strident grotto. 4.5 Anxious fibs

items.body: Review by alainPP — 1. "The Storm" captures a mood of melancholy?oozing guitar tones followed by percussive pounding and Riccardo's vintage keyboards launching the final solo. The lead guitar work is meltingly smooth and delicate?a real treat.2. "Sandsend" follows, with guitar supported by keyboards once again?Steve's guitar (the veteran member, if I'm not mistaken). It's a sweet, ambient, dreamy melody that casts a spell without overcomplicating things. Daniele's keyboard and percussion work is worth noting here.3. "Red Dragon" appeals immediately with its Celtic opening featuring bagpipes. I don't see a red dragon on the horizon, but rather a tune oscillating between Ireland, Scotland, and the Maghreb?a delicate blend of sounds that unite different worlds, which is what matters most. The guitars feel airy, plaintive, and hopeful, drifting into a dreamlike state. It features a radiant horn outro.4. "The Roaring Waves" arrives; if that isn't Steve playing, then it certainly sounds like him?delivering a magnificent, warm arpeggio over a chord progression reminiscent of classic Genesis (see if you can spot the influence). Those crystalline notes, plucked one by one, evoke an illustrious past. The track builds into a breathtaking solo?simple yet intense. The mood turns solemn, like a funeral march, with guitars?both acoustic and electric?softening before leading the listener into a neo-classical melodic passage; a gentle finale.5. "K-129" has a Gabriel-esque vibe?reminiscent of his world music work, specifically the *Birdy* soundtrack?creating an immersive, tribal atmosphere. There's a touch of 80s-era Genesis synth?or even Tangerine Dream?in that repetitive keyboard line. Daniele's dark percussion kicks off the guitar's wandering melody, building into a mantra-like crescendo. The track wouldn't be complete without that heart-wrenching solo?classic-era Marillion style: simple yet flawless.6. "The Black Sea" sees Leon on percussion?specifically a Hang drum with a touch of vintage vinyl crackle. The guitar tone is Floyd-esque and atmospheric, offering an enchanting, cinematic bluesy melody that feels like the perfect soundtrack for a TV series. Steve launches into a melancholic solo over a rising build-up?yet another one?that elevates the emotion to heavenly heights. It ends with a decrescendo accompanied by crackling sounds.7. "Pacific Coast Highway" marks a radical shift in sound; the American West comes alive with a festive, Western-rock vibe?think Chet Atkins?that makes you want to dance energetically and forget your age. Steve Hackett has a blast on the harmonica?at least you know it's him?while Riccardo treats us to an organ solo that harks back to the instrument's glory days. I detect a hint of Dire Straits in the fiery guitar work; my legs start moving and breaking into a dance. Halfway through, the acoustic guitar takes on a growly, Supertramp-esque edge before shifting into a linear guitar solo?not technical, just brimming with feeling and resonance. The finale is Oldfield-esque and pastoral, featuring a sensual, bucolic choir and a flute appearing out of nowhere to close the track.(3.5)

The first album not to feature Brent Hinds after his departure then untimely death, lyrically the album deals with loss and the difficulties surrounding it. Overall lyrically it's some of their most poignant and creative. The added use of keyboards to their sound, while present before is now heightened with new member Jo�o Nogueira displaying some nice organ pedals and synth leads, while Nick Johnston has a similar style to the late Hinds, but has a uniqueness in his lead playing. While it's sad not to hear Hinds soulful vocals, Brann Dailor & Troy Sander's vocals are pretty impressive at times, but they do show weakness as well. items.body: Review by Prog Dog — On my way over to finally dig into Neal Morse's album for my first review, I stumbled across an email I'd overlooked about his brother Alan's recent solo album. My curiosity got the better of me, and I was not disappointed. In fact, I feel like I've made a new guitar friend. Alan is a serious axe player and a very good songwriter to boot, and I've been quite taken by his soulful style and technique throughout this tastefully produced disc. This also proves the lyric from his title track, "Everyday Is Insane." Not really, but thank goodness for spontaneity.This is his second solo album (I haven't yet heard the first), and it's an impressive showcase of the man's very creative and understated solo work. There's very little repetitiveness or redundancy across this collection of eleven tunes, testifying to the abundance of raw source material he is drawing on here. If you're not fond of a song or a moment in a song, just wait a a minute and something completely fresh will come up next. After a few listens I find that I might not be in the mood for a track or two but I generally enjoy it all. He calls on a long list of friends and family to help out on various instruments and background vocals, and there's probably no shortage of familiar names here, least of all his brother Neal (by the way is Neal the big brother? or the little brother??). Tony Levin's presence caught my eye right away. And daughter Julia sings on "Making Up My Heart," which strikes me as a really sweet and personal touch, and a lovely reminder that the line of musical talent runs deep through the Morse family.This is essential listening for any serious Spock's Beard fan, of course, since that's Alan's main gig, and most of the band helps out.To me, though, this is a guitarist's album. Oh, wait, it's a real treat for drummers as well. The drum kits sound amazing and sit tight and loud in the mix throughout, and there's this ripper of a solo at the end of "Making Up My Heart". On the drum throne are some notable players: Simon Phillips, Jimmy Keegan, John Morse and, of course, Nick D'Virgilio.Alan isn't really lead-singer material in the sense of fronting a top-tier band on the world stage, but in a personable singer-songwriter setting, he's more than pleasant company for the ears.Since Alan is proficient in almost any stringed instrument, and he plays more than just guitar on the album. Not sure exactly how many but I heard bouzouki, cello, mandolin, and electric sitar. Not the most attractive album cover, but once you hear what's under the hood, you'll warm right up to it. There are almost party-rock vibes to some of the album, think Van Halen or that unmistakable '80s energy. I hear hints of classic Saga and perhaps '80s Rush as well. It's a thoroughly enjoyable listen for a guitarist and prog fan like me.Prog Dog score: 3.5 out of 5 &/or 3 out of 5 for the progarchives system.
